parts.label: b.i
parts.display_text: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, show that the energy in state n is Eₙ = −ke²/(2a₀n²). Here a₀ is the Bohr radius and k is the Coulomb constant.

answer.text: Substitute rₙ = a₀n² into the supplied E = −ke²/(2r): Eₙ = −ke²/(2a₀n²).

source.url: https://www.tsokosphysics.com/content/4 worksheets/Topic E/The Bohr model.pdf
source.collection_label: K. A. Tsokos · The Bohr model
source.title: The Bohr model

bridge_result.text: Substitute rₙ = a₀n² into the supplied E = −ke²/(2r): Eₙ = −ke²/(2a₀n²).

parts.given_text: Use the classical energy E = −ke²/(2r), and the Bohr relations rₙ = a₀n² and mₑvₙrₙ = nh/(2π).

parts.label: b.ii
parts.display_text: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, show that the electron speed in state n is vₙ = h/(2πmₑa₀n). Here mₑ is the electron mass and a₀ is the Bohr radius.

answer.text: mₑvₙrₙ = nh/(2π) gives vₙ = nh/(2πmₑa₀n²) = h/(2πmₑa₀n).

source.url: https://www.tsokosphysics.com/content/4 worksheets/Topic E/The Bohr model.pdf
source.collection_label: K. A. Tsokos · The Bohr model
source.title: The Bohr model

bridge_result.text: mₑvₙrₙ = nh/(2π) gives vₙ = nh/(2πmₑa₀n²) = h/(2πmₑa₀n).

parts.given_text: Use the Bohr relations rₙ = a₀n² and mₑvₙrₙ = nh/(2π).

parts.label: b.iii
parts.display_text: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, show that the orbital frequency in state n is fₙ = h/(4π²mₑa₀²n³).

source.url: https://www.tsokosphysics.com/content/4 worksheets/Topic E/The Bohr model.pdf
source.collection_label: K. A. Tsokos · The Bohr model
source.title: The Bohr model

bridge_result.text: fₙ = vₙ/(2πrₙ) = [h/(2πmₑa₀n)]/(2πa₀n²) = h/(4π²mₑa₀²n³).

parts.given_text: Use rₙ = a₀n², vₙ = h/(2πmₑa₀n), and the supplied circular-motion relation f = v/(2πr).

parts.label: c.ii

answer.text: The photon energy is approximately ke²/(a₀n³). Hence f = ke²/(ha₀n³) = h/(4π²mₑa₀²n³).

source.url: https://www.tsokosphysics.com/content/4 worksheets/Topic E/The Bohr model.pdf
source.collection_label: K. A. Tsokos · The Bohr model
source.title: The Bohr model

bridge_result.text: The photon energy is approximately ke²/(a₀n³). Hence f = ke²/(ha₀n³) = h/(4π²mₑa₀²n³).

parts.given_text: For large n, use the mathematical result 1/n² − 1/(n+1)² ≈ 2/n³.

answer.text: For large n this equals the classical orbital frequency from (b)(iii), illustrating Bohr’s correspondence principle: quantum predictions approach the classical result in this limit.
